steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on cross-lingual transfer with LLMs by merging adapters: the idea is that task ability and language ability are connected, and we get the target-language adapter by merging. Cover related approaches, the method, and headline results.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Multilingual models and the need for cross-lingual transfer
- Existing cross-lingual transfer approaches (use English ability; decouple-and-merge)
- Our view: task and language ability are interconnected; the adapter-space analogy
- AdaMergeX: reference task + source-language fine-tuning + merging
- Structure-adaptive merging
- Evaluation and main results

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Multilingual models, cross-lingual transfer
  - conventional: mBERT, XLM, XLM-R; multilingual LLMs: ChatGPT, PaLM2, Llama2 (cite each); growing multilingual needs
  - low-resource languages: task training data scarce, fine-tuning impractical (cite)
  - cross-lingual transfer: extend task-solving ability from source language to many target languages (cite)
- Existing approaches
  - transfer "task-ability" from source to target language ("language ability")
  - some don't improve language ability directly; use English ability: translation, representation alignment, prompting for LLMs (cite each)
  - some intertwine the two: fine-tune on translated parallel corpora (cite)
  - others decouple task/language ability, enhance separately, then merge (cite)
  - but ignores interdependence; any task is expressed in some language -> can't isolate
- Our view
  - language ability and task ability inherently interconnected
  - task ability tied to source language; language ability = capacity gap between target and source language
  - like "king-queen=man-woman" in word embeddings (cite)
  - assume divergence between LLMs fine-tuned in different languages on a task has same distribution across tasks
  - PEFT: {read}^{\,fr}-{read}^{\,en}={math}^{\,fr}-{math}^{\,en} in adapter space; read/math tasks, fr/en languages
  - Figure 2 left
- AdaMergeX (Adaptive Adapter Merging), Figure 2 right
  - reference task gives target-source language divergence; easy to access for high- and low-resource languages, e.g. causal language modeling
  - fine-tune LLM on target task in source language
  - merge language ability + task ability -> adapters for target task in target language
- Structure-adaptive merging
  - previous: linear combination of models/adapters (cite)
  - merging should match how adapters are integrated with the model
  - adaptively select merging for LoRA, (IA) 3, Adapter, Prefix-Tuning (cite each)
- Evaluation
  - multilingual tasks, 12 languages, high- to low-resource
  - beats SOTA: model merging, prompting, general adapter merging
  - vs MAD-X (two adapters for task/language): 8.0\% and 15.9\% absolute on XCOPA and XQuAD with XLM-R
  - vs Arimerge (SOTA adapter merging): 31.1\% relative on average, all languages and tasks, Llama2
  - ablation: consistent across backbones, source languages, reference tasks

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Multilingual NLP models have gained a lot of attention because of the growing need for multilingual requirements. These include conventional models like mBERT, XLM and XLM-R, and also recent multilingual large language models (LLMs) like ChatGPT, PaLM2 and Llama2. To further improve the model's multilingual capability, especially when training data of certain tasks for low-resource languages is scarce and fine-tuning is impractical, cross-lingual transfer is introduced, which extends the task-solving ability in a source language to a wide range of target languages.

Basically, cross-lingual transfer tries to transfer the ability to solve a certain task ("task-ability") from a source language to a particular target language ("language ability"). Some cross-lingual transfer techniques do not directly improve the language ability in specific languages. They instead use the language ability in English for multilingual tasks, with methods like translation, representation alignment, or prompting methods developed for LLMs. Some works mix these two abilities together and use translated parallel corpora for fine-tuning.

On the other hand, some studies focus directly on improving the language abilities in target languages, and they try to decouple task ability and language ability, improve them separately, and then merge them. But this ignores that task ability and language ability depend on each other. Any specific task is expressed in a particular language, so the two abilities cannot be clearly separated from each other.

In this work, we argue that language ability and task ability are connected in nature. They should not be separated; instead, task ability belongs to the source language, while language ability means the capacity gap between the target language and the source language. Similar to the famous equation "king-queen=man-woman" in the word embedding space, we assume that the differences between LLMs fine-tuned in different languages on a particular task follow the same distribution across different tasks. For parameter-efficient fine-tuning, the equation becomes {read}^{\,fr}-{read}^{\,en}={math}^{\,fr}-{math}^{\,en} in the adapter space, where read and math are two tasks, and fr and en are the two languages of the tasks. As the left side of Figure 2 shows, in the adapter space the divergence between the target language and the source language on the target task follows the same distribution as the divergence on the reference task.

- AdaMergeX (Adaptive Adapter Merging), Figure 2 right
  - reference task gives target-source language divergence; easy to access for high- and low-resource languages, e.g. causal language modeling
  - fine-tune LLM on target task in source language
  - merge language ability + task ability -> adapters for target task in target language
- Structure-adaptive merging
  - previous: linear combination of models/adapters
  - merging should match how adapters are integrated with the model
  - adaptively select merging for LoRA, (IA) 3, Adapter, Prefix-Tuning
- Evaluation
  - multilingual tasks, 12 languages, high- to low-resource
  - beats SOTA: model merging, prompting, general adapter merging
  - vs MAD-X (two adapters for task/language): 8.0\% and 15.9\% absolute on XCOPA and XQuAD with XLM-R
  - vs Arimerge (SOTA adapter merging): 31.1\% relative on average, all languages and tasks, Llama2
  - ablation: consistent across backbones, source languages, reference tasks

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Multilingual NLP models have gained a lot of attention because of the growing need for multilingual requirements. These include conventional models like mBERT, XLM and XLM-R, and also recent multilingual large language models (LLMs) like ChatGPT, PaLM2 and Llama2. To further improve the model's multilingual capability, especially when training data of certain tasks for low-resource languages is scarce and fine-tuning is impractical, cross-lingual transfer is introduced, which extends the task-solving ability in a source language to a wide range of target languages.

Basically, cross-lingual transfer tries to transfer the ability to solve a certain task ("task-ability") from a source language to a particular target language ("language ability"). Some cross-lingual transfer techniques do not directly improve the language ability in specific languages. They instead use the language ability in English for multilingual tasks, with methods like translation, representation alignment, or prompting methods developed for LLMs. Some works mix these two abilities together and use translated parallel corpora for fine-tuning.

On the other hand, some studies focus directly on improving the language abilities in target languages, and they try to decouple task ability and language ability, improve them separately, and then merge them. But this ignores that task ability and language ability depend on each other. Any specific task is expressed in a particular language, so the two abilities cannot be clearly separated from each other.

In this work, we argue that language ability and task ability are connected in nature. They should not be separated; instead, task ability belongs to the source language, while language ability means the capacity gap between the target language and the source language. Similar to the famous equation "king-queen=man-woman" in the word embedding space, we assume that the differences between LLMs fine-tuned in different languages on a particular task follow the same distribution across different tasks. For parameter-efficient fine-tuning, the equation becomes {read}^{\,fr}-{read}^{\,en}={math}^{\,fr}-{math}^{\,en} in the adapter space, where read and math are two tasks, and fr and en are the two languages of the tasks. As the left side of Figure 2 shows, in the adapter space the divergence between the target language and the source language on the target task follows the same distribution as the divergence on the reference task.

So we propose to do cross-lingual transfer through Adaptive Adapter Merging (AdaMergeX) using this relation, as shown on the right side of Figure 2. Specifically, we introduce a reference task, and from it we get the divergence between the target language and the source language. The reference task can be an easy to access task for both high-resource and low-resource languages, like causal language modeling. We also fine-tune LLMs on the target task in the source language. Finally, we merge the language ability and the task ability and get the adapters of the target task in the target language.

Also, previous studies combine models or adapters with a linear combination, but we argue that the model merging method should match the way adapters are integrated with language models. So we design a structure-adaptive adapter merging method that can adaptively pick the merging method for LoRA, (IA) 3, Adapter, Prefix-Tuning etc.

We evaluate AdaMergeX on many multilingual tasks in 12 languages, covering a wide resource range from high-resource to low-resource languages. The evaluation shows that AdaMergeX always outperforms other state-of-the-art methods, including model merging, prompting, and general adapter merging methods. Compared to MAD-X, which separates task and language ability with two adapters, AdaMergeX gets 8.0\% and 15.9\% absolute improvement on XCOPA and XQuAD with XLM-R. Compared to the state-of-the-art adapter merging method Arimerge, AdaMergeX gets 31.1\% relative improvement on average in all languages and all tasks with Llama2. The ablation analysis also shows that AdaMergeX works consistently well with different backbone models, source languages, and reference tasks.

But this ignores that task ability and language ability depend on each other. Any specific task is expressed in a particular language, so the two abilities cannot be clearly separated from each other.

In this work, we argue that language ability and task ability are connected in nature. steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Multilingual NLP models, including conventional models such as mBERT [1], XLM [2] and XLM-R [3], as well as recent multilingual large language models (LLMs) like ChatGPT [4], PaLM2 [5] and Llama2 [6], have gained significant attention given the growing need for multilingual requirements. To further enhance the model's multilingual capability, particularly when training data of certain tasks for low-resource languages is scarce and fine-tuning becomes impractical [7], cross-lingual transfer is introduced to extend the task-solving ability in a source language to a wide range of target languages [8,9,10].

Essentially, cross-lingual transfer aims to transfer the ability to solve a certain task ("task-ability") from a source language to a particular target language ("language ability"). Some cross-lingual transfer techniques do not directly improve the language ability in specific languages. Instead, they utilize the language ability in English for multilingual tasks by employing methods such as translation [11,12], representation alignment [13,14,15], or prompting methods developed for LLMs [16,17,18]. Some works intertwine the two abilities and use translated parallel corpora for fine-tuning [19,20,21].

In contrast, some studies directly focus on enhancing the language abilities in target languages, so they try to decouple task ability and language ability, enhance them separately, and then merge them [22,23,24]. However, such an approach overlooks the intrinsic interdependence between task ability and language ability. Since any specific task is expressed in a particular language, the two abilities cannot be distinctly isolated from one another.

In this work, we argue that language ability and task ability are inherently interconnected. Instead of separating one from the other, we hold that task ability is affiliated with the source language, while language ability refers to the capacity gap between the target language and the source language. In line with the famous equation "king-queen=man-woman" in the word embedding space [25], we assume that the divergences between LLMs fine-tuned in different languages on a particular task follow the same distribution across diverse tasks. For parameter-efficient fine-tuning, the equation becomes {read}^{\,fr}-{read}^{\,en}={math}^{\,fr}-{math}^{\,en} in the adapter space, where read and math refer to two tasks, and fr and en indicate the two languages of the corresponding tasks. As shown in the left side of Figure 2, in the adapter space, the divergence between the target language and the source language on the target task follows the same distribution as the divergence on the reference task.

Therefore, we propose to accomplish cross-lingual transfer through Adaptive Adapter Merging (AdaMergeX) based on this relation, as shown in the right side of Figure 2. Specifically, we introduce a reference task from which we obtain the divergence between the target language and the source language. Such a reference task can be an easily accessible task for both high-resource and low-resource languages, such as causal language modeling. In addition, we fine-tune LLMs on the target task in the source language. Finally, by merging the language ability and the task ability, we obtain the adapters of the target task in the target language.

Furthermore, unlike previous studies that combine models or adapters through a linear combination [26,27,24], we argue that the model merging method should align with the way adapters are integrated with language models. We therefore design a structure-adaptive adapter merging method, which can adaptively select merging methods for LoRA [28], (IA) 3 [29], Adapter [30], Prefix-Tuning [31] etc.

We evaluate AdaMergeX on a wide range of multilingual tasks spanning 12 languages, covering a broad resource spectrum from high-resource to low-resource languages. Our evaluation shows that AdaMergeX consistently outperforms other state-of-the-art methods, including model merging, prompting, and general adapter merging methods. Notably, compared to MAD-X [22], which separates task and language ability with two adapters, AdaMergeX achieves 8.0\% and 15.9\% absolute improvement on XCOPA and XQuAD respectively with XLM-R. Compared with the state-of-the-art adapter merging method Arimerge [27], AdaMergeX achieves 31.1\% relative improvement on average across all languages and all tasks with Llama2. Moreover, the ablation analysis shows that AdaMergeX performs consistently well with different backbone models, source languages, and reference tasks.
